accepted.question_text: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets. For a feasible integer n, meaning a positive even integer n >= 20 with n != 22, let C_n denote the set of all fullerenes with exactly n vertices, considered up to graph isomorphism as fullerene isomers. Can one design a computationally efficient procedure that samples uniformly from the fullerene isomers in C_n, so that every isomer in C_n is selected with the same probability?
accepted.context_brief: Uniform random generation of fullerene isomers

accepted.question_text: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets. For a feasible n, meaning a positive even integer n >= 20 with n != 22, let T_n be the unique dual graph of such a fullerene. A generalized Stone-Wales (gSW) path in T_n is a path (v_1, ..., v_{2w}) of odd length 2w - 1 such that v_1 and v_{2w} have degree 5, v_2 and v_{2w-1} have degree 6, all vertices are distinct, and (v_i, v_{i+2}) is an edge for every i = 1, ..., 2w - 2. Since a gSW operation can be applied only when such a path exists, which fullerene isomers do not permit any generalized Stone-Wales operation at all?
accepted.context_brief: Classification of fullerenes without gSW moves

evidence.quote: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets.
Thus, we define a positive even integer n ≥ 20, n ̸= 22, as feasible.

Since fullerenes are 3-connected, Whitney’s theorem cf. [25] ensures that their dual graph is unique. A dual fullerene, denoted by Tn , can also be viewed as an element of the set of all convex triangulations of the sphere, as described in [19].

Definition 1. For a feasible n and w ∈ N, w ≥ 2, let a Cn -isomer with dual graph Tn be given. We call (a) a path (v1 , . . . , v2w ) with vi ∈ V (Tn ) a gSW path of length 2w − 1, if the following in Tn holds: • v1 and v2w have degree 5, • v2 and v2w−1 have degree 6, • vi ̸= vj for i ̸= j, • (vi , vi+2 ) ∈ E (Tn ) for all i = 1, . . . , 2w − 2.
From this definition, it follows that the existence of a gSW path in a fullerene is necessary to apply the gSW operation to this fullerene.
Open Problem 2. Identify all fullerenes that do not permit a gSW operation.

accepted.question_text: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets. Let C_n denote the set of all fullerenes with exactly n vertices, and let T_n be a random dual graph of a fullerene in C_n. For any dual fullerene graph G with adjacency matrix A and degree matrix D, define its (1/2, 1/4)-character by ch_{1/2,1/4}(G) := tr(exp((1/2)A + (1/4)D)). Does the normalized quantity [ch_{1/2,1/4}(T_n) - min_H ch_{1/2,1/4}(H)] / [max_H ch_{1/2,1/4}(H) - min_H ch_{1/2,1/4}(H)] converge as n tends to infinity, where the minimum and maximum are taken over dual graphs H of fullerenes in C_n? If the limit exists, what is its explicit form or limiting distribution?

evidence.quote: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets.
Let Cn denote the set of all fullerenes with exactly n vertices. This set can be partitioned into equivalence classes under graph isomorphisms, with each class referred to as a Cn -isomer.

The subgraph of Tn induced by the vertices of degree five captures the connectivity between the pentagons, while the subgraph induced by vertices of degree six represents the connectivity between hexagons. We denote these graphs by Tn5 and Tn6 , respectively.

The lexicografically smallest spiral is then selected. The positions of the twelve 5’s in this spiral provide the locations of the pentagonal faces yielding a final sequence of length 12 representing the fullerene.
Listing fullerenes in Cn in lexicographical order, based on the positions of their pentagons within the spiral, provides a compact and interpretable representation and enumeration of fullerenes.
Therefore, when referring to Cn,j , we mean the j th isomer in the lexicographical order of all Cn -isomers, based on their smallest pentagonal position sequence.

Definition 2. For a feasible n, let Tn6 be the hexagonal dual graph of a fullerene in Cn , and let t, r1 , r2 , r3 ∈ N0 , r1 ≥ r2 ≥ r3 , ri + rj ≤ t − 1 for i ̸= j. We call a connected component of Tn6 (a) a t-triangle, for t = 0, if it is a single vertex, and for t > 0, if • it has t2 triangles as inner faces, and • it has 1/2 (t + 1)(t + 2) vertices, three of which are of degree two, 3(t − 1) vertices of degree four, and the remaining vertices of degree six. The vertices of degree two are called corners of the t-triangle.
Definition 4. For a given Tn6 we call the set of components of the graph generated following Construction 1 a cut-partition of Tn6 .
Conjecture 1. C56,622 and C80,31924 are the only fullerenes whose cut-partition consists of t-triangles only.

evidence.quote: A fullerene is a convex, 3-regular polytope consisting only of pentagonal and hexagonal facets.
Thus, we define a positive even integer n ≥ 20, n ̸= 22, as feasible.

Since fullerenes are 3-connected, Whitney’s theorem cf. [25] ensures that their dual graph is unique. A dual fullerene, denoted by Tn , can also be viewed as an element of the set of all convex triangulations of the sphere, as described in [19].

The subgraph of Tn induced by the vertices of degree five captures the connectivity between the pentagons, while the subgraph induced by vertices of degree six represents the connectivity between hexagons. We denote these graphs by Tn5 and Tn6 , respectively.

Definition 1. For a feasible n and w ∈ N, w ≥ 2, let a Cn -isomer with dual graph Tn be given. We call (a) a path (v1 , . . . , v2w ) with vi ∈ V (Tn ) a gSW path of length 2w − 1, if the following in Tn holds: • v1 and v2w have degree 5, • v2 and v2w−1 have degree 6, • vi ̸= vj for i ̸= j, • (vi , vi+2 ) ∈ E (Tn ) for all i = 1, . . . , 2w − 2.

Definition 2. For a feasible n, let Tn6 be the hexagonal dual graph of a fullerene in Cn , and let t, r1 , r2 , r3 ∈ N0 , r1 ≥ r2 ≥ r3 , ri + rj ≤ t − 1 for i ̸= j. We call a connected component of Tn6 (a) a t-triangle, for t = 0, if it is a single vertex, and for t > 0, if • it has t2 triangles as inner faces, and • it has 1/2 (t + 1)(t + 2) vertices, three of which are of degree two, 3(t − 1) vertices of degree four, and the remaining vertices of degree six. The vertices of degree two are called corners of the t-triangle.

Definition 2. For a feasible n, let Tn6 be the hexagonal dual graph of a fullerene in Cn , and let t, r1 , r2 , r3 ∈ N0 , r1 ≥ r2 ≥ r3 , ri + rj ≤ t − 1 for i ̸= j. We call a connected component of Tn6 (b) a (t, (r1 , r2 , r3 ))-triangle, if it is a t-triangle in which the vertices of r1 -, r2 -, and r3 -triangles at the corners have been deleted. Edges between vertices whose degree decreased due to the deletion are called open edges.
Definition 3. A vertex v ∈ V (Tn6 ) is called a 2-facet vertex or 3-facet vertex, if v is a boundary vertex of two or three facets of Tn6 larger than a triangle, respectively.

Construction 1. Let Tn6 be the hexagonal subgraph of a dual fullerene Tn . Transform Tn6 by applying the following two operations: 1. For every 2-facet vertex v ∈ V (Tn6 ), apply the following cut operation: (i) Choose a minimal set of edges incident to v such that deleting these edges makes v a boundary vertex of only one facet larger than a triangle. (ii) After deleting these edges, insert a new vertex ṽ into the graph. (iii) Reinsert the removed edges so that ṽ becomes the endpoint of these edges, replacing v.

2. Let v1 , . . . , vl ∈ V (T̃n6 ) be all vertices of degree 5 in T̃n6 . While vertices of degree 5 exists, perform the following procedure: (i) Find a pair of vertices (vi , vj ), i, j = 1, . . . , l, i ̸= j, on a connected component CC of T̃n6 , such that the shortest path p = (vi , . . . , vj ) between them is minimal among the shortest paths between any other pairs of vertices of degree 5, and such that the edges of p surround solely triangular facets. The path p divides CC into two parts, denoted by CC1 and CC2 . (ii) Delete all edges with one endpoint in, say, CC2 , and the other endpoint being a vertex on the path p. (iii) For every vertex v in p, add a new vertex ṽe to T̃n6 . (iv) Add edges between these new vertices, replicating the edges of the original path p. (v) Reintroduce all edges deleted in step (ii), replacing the original endpoint v with its corresponding copy ṽe.
Definition 4. For a given Tn6 we call the set of components of the graph generated following Construction 1 a cut-partition of Tn6 .

Conjecture 2. Let Tn6 , for a feasible n, be the hexagonal subgraph of Tn . The cut-partition of Tn6 consists solely of elements that are either t-triangles or (t, (r1 , r2 , r3 ))-triangles if and only if Tn contains no gSW path – with the exception that the cut-partition contains only 0-triangles.
